title: Such a Doggone Good Feeling
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Using Fred Rogers as a model, Stuart draws two lessons for secondary teachers from Mister Rogers' repeated line, "It's such a good feeling." First, Rogers made the implicit explicit, naming feelings and experiences aloud rather than assuming viewers already understood them, which Stuart argues is an underrated, high-leverage teaching move given how often secondary classrooms suffer from insufficiently explicit instruction. Second, Rogers demonstrated unshakeable confidence that what he offered was a timeless good, even while working through a medium, television, he knew could also harm children. Stuart extends this to teaching: school, like television, is one of the few remaining cultural commonplaces, wrought with real problems yet still fertile soil for helping young people flourish. He closes by urging teachers to actively remind themselves of the good feeling of the work, since neither the school system, the broader culture, nor students themselves will reliably do that reminding.
points: Rogers' habit of naming feelings explicitly ("that's a good feeling") models an underused instructional move: secondary classrooms often suffer from too little explicit instruction and too much assumed understanding.
Stuart draws a direct parallel between television as a flawed-but-valuable cultural commonplace and school as the same for today's students.
The essay argues teachers must self-generate reminders of the goodness of their work, since the school system and students won't reliably supply that affirmation.
Confidence in the value of one's discipline, modeled after Rogers, is framed as a teachable disposition rather than an accident of personality.
quotes: Rather than assuming everyone feels the same as him and is able to identify feelings he's able to identify, Rogers explicitly says, again and again: "Do you feel that feeling? That's a good one.
The bulk of our classrooms suffer for lack of explicit instruction. We are tragically presumptuous about what our students understand.
And second, Rogers is So. Doggone. Confident. He knows that what he's offering his students — the kids viewing his show — is a timeless good.

We work in a medium — school — that's one of the few remaining commonplaces in the communities wherein we live. Television's commonplaceness is gone now, replaced by an algorithmically individualized, numberless, creators-driven Internet.

No — just like Rogers was responsible for reminding himself of the good feelings possible in television, so too are we responsible, in a world gone mad, for reminding ourselves of the Why behind what we do.
